title: Before a paper bot gets real money, what does it have to prove? My three rules, and where they're weak
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Saw the thread here about paper trading 31,000 strategies for 8 months and moving the best 3 to real money. It made me write down my own bar, because I've been vague about it for too long.

What I use right now:

1. Time, not trade count. A rule has to run on paper through a stretch the backtest never saw, including at least one ugly week, before I even consider it. Fifty clean trades in a calm month prove very little.

2. Paper has to look like the backtest. If the paper fills drift away from what the backtest assumed (options especially, where a lot of backtests quietly take the middle of the spread and paper pays the ask), that gap is the answer, and it's rarely a good one.

3. I have to be able to say why it works in one sentence. If the only reason is "the optimizer found it", it goes back on the shelf.

Where I think these are weak: rule 1 has no hard number, and picking the best 3 out of thousands is a selection problem of its own that a few paper months only partly fix.

How Quantradin helps with this: it's my project, and this middle stage is where it lives. You describe the rule in plain English or paste the code, it backtests without look-ahead, and the survivors run as paper bots on live prices, with options filled at the bid or the ask, never the middle. You can also connect your AI (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, Codex...) and let it run its ideas through the same test. I built it, it's free, and it's paper money only: [quantradin.com](http://quantradin.com)

So, for the room: what's your bar before a bot gets real money? A number of months, a number of trades, a drawdown it has to survive, or something else?

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: I would make the bar depend on evidence, not a universal month or trade count. If you select the best 3 from thousands, their paper phase should begin only after selection and use a precommitted promotion test, such as a confidence bound on expectancy after costs plus a maximum-drawdown limit. For options, bid-or-ask fills are conservative but incomplete; reject or resize trades when contemporaneous quoted size could not fill the order. I would also define “one ugly week” in advance using volatility or spread percentiles, otherwise it can be declared sufficient after the fact.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the selection point is the one I keep dodging. starting the paper clock only after the 3 are picked at least stops me counting months they spent being chosen. a confidence bound after costs is fairer than my one ugly week, though at 30 or 40 trades the bound is so wide most rules fail it, which may just be the honest answer.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
I'd separate the decision to go live into two independent gates.

The first is statistical: does the frozen strategy have enough genuinely new evidence after costs to justify taking risk?

The second is operational: can the execution system fail safely?

I'm building TIYlab, a non-custodial Bitcoin portfolio automation project, and this distinction is particularly important in our work.

A strategy might pass its forward validation and still be unsafe to deploy.

For example, what happens if an order reaches the exchange but the acknowledgement never comes back?

Or if the bot restarts while an order is partially filled?

Before allowing new decisions, I'd require the engine to reconcile its local state with actual orders and positions.

I'd also test stale market data, rejected orders and loss of connectivity.

None of those tests proves a profitable edge, but failing them should prevent live activation regardless of the backtest.

I'd keep the statistical and operational results separate rather than combining them into a single readiness score.

Does QuanTradin plan to evaluate execution failure scenarios, or is its validation currently focused on strategy performance?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the operational gate is the one I underweighted. all three of my rules are statistical, and a paper bot never meets a rejected order or a half filled exit, so it can pass everything and still fall over on day one. agree on frozen too, any tweak after the paper clock starts should reset it.

replies.author: Maleficent-Success-6
replies.body:
Exactly. And the good news is that you don't necessarily need real money to start testing that operational gate.

You can deliberately inject rejected orders, delayed acknowledgements, partial fills, stale data and connection drops into the paper execution layer.

The important part is checking what the engine does afterward, not just whether it detects the failure.

For example, after an ambiguous order response, I'd block new trading decisions until the exchange state and local state are reconciled.

And I agree on resetting the validation clock after a strategy change. Otherwise, forward testing gradually becomes another optimization process.

One distinction I'd keep, though: passing simulated failure tests demonstrates recovery logic, not that real exchange behavior has been fully validated. That still requires carefully controlled live execution.

comments.author: LuckOrEdge
comments.body: I've never thought about your first point, but I think it makes sense. I usually go by the amount of trades in order to find statistical significance. Your point is that statistical significance is not the only important factor, but survivability in different market environments are also essential. Very interesting... how long of a stretch do you usually do?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, sample size alone will pass a rule that only ever met one kind of market. 200 trades from one calm stretch tell you less than 60 spread over a selloff, a grind up and a flat summer.

comments.author: fomoz
